title: Sprocket & Sprout
pitch: Take over an old keeper's clockwork farm and bring it back machine by machine, until it runs itself like a music box.
number: 2.1 "Overseas": a merchant ship buys your exports
about: You arrive in the valley town of Thistlewick to take over the old keeper's clockwork farm. The works stand rusted around one preserving crock still bubbling on its last beans. Bring them back machine by machine: within minutes an arm you restored is carrying pickles to the shipping crate, a gleaner picks the field you planted, and the keeper's water wheel turns the grist mill by the river.

Every machine tells you what it is doing and why it stopped, so a stuck line is a puzzle you can solve instead of a mystery. The town is your customer: fill its orders, rank up with each business, and bring back the mill, the waterworks, the street lamps, the tram and the clock.
Hand farming is still here whenever you want it, and the morning summary names yesterday's biggest bottleneck.

2.1, "Overseas", opens the Harbor: late in the game a merchant ship, the Copper Gull, calls at the beach pier with a manifest from a port across the sea, asking for goods in amounts only a factory can make, like 300 iron bars or 2,000 glass. Fill it and climb six ranks, from Dockhand to Merchant Prince.
madeWith: TypeScript and Canvas, no engine. Code written with Claude Opus from my design docs; pixel art made with PixelLab; sound made procedurally.
platforms: Browser (installable as an app), Windows installer

title: Arcwarm
pitch: A Quake Live lightning-gun duel against a bot, with Halo gravity and shields. The duel is the warm-up.
about: A 2–5 minute aim warm-up you play as a game. You and a bot share the same movement and the same lightning gun, so you track while you move and dodge, and the bot's beam punishes predictable movement.

Halo gravity and air control, Quake Live gun and hitbox numbers. Lifesteal is on by default: every hit heals the shooter, so a fight is decided by who misses more. The bot's aim comes from perception delay and your movement, not dice, across five levels from Easy to Nightmare.
Two maps: Pinehollow, a forest bowl with a treehouse, a shrine and a man cannon, and the White Room, a plain grid with ramps.
madeWith: JavaScript and Three.js. Code written with Claude Opus from my design notes.

title: Overgrowth
pitch: Raid the jungle by day and carry home what you can. Hold the Heartwood by night. Survive ten nights and find out what happened to the 1931 expedition.
about: By day you hack through the jungle with a machete, forage the forest floor, and search old camps, wrecks, temples and root caches for what's inside. Everything you carry weighs something, so you choose what to bring home before dusk. At camp you craft it into towers, barricades and traps at the Workbench, Fire Pit and Tinker's Bench, and build them around the Heartwood, the glowing shrine at your camp.

At dusk the Blight crawls out of rifts in the forest and looks for the side your towers cover least. The Heartwood can only feed so many roots, so every defence is a budget call, and each kind of Blight shrugs off some damage types and breaks under others. Hold until dawn. Each night is harder, every fifth night brings a boss, and the Rot Mother comes on night 10. Endless mode keeps going after that.

Along the way came Blight Blooms that open new lanes unless you cut them down (0.6), three difficulties and a Field Guide (0.7), and the drowned grove, a second region of black water and mangroves with its own rift (0.9).

1.0, "The Lost Expedition", turned the day into a scavenging run and added a story: twelve torn pages from a 1931 expedition, three seals that put rifts to sleep, grafts for your towers, a radio that calls supply drops, the Rot spreading from the rifts, and two endings. It also added key rebinding, captions, colour-blind outlines, partial gamepad support, twenty achievements and a daily vigil. Since then, 1.0.1 halved what everything weighs, 1.0.2 got rid of the random freezes, and 1.0.3 made the satchel drag-and-drop, lets you clad the Coffer in iron and brass for up to 120 slots, and made the Blight a fifth tougher.
madeWith: JavaScript and Three.js. Code written with Claude Opus; surfaces and foliage generated with Flux, the hero models built in Blender from Python scripts, and the sound synthesized live.
platforms: Browser (desktop, keyboard and mouse; partial gamepad)

title: Pixel RTS
pitch: Mine ore, pump oil, build armies and capture cities. Win by conquest, by science, or by holding the map. Up to six players online, nothing to install.
about: A top-down pixel-art RTS inspired by The Conquerors 3 and Strategema on Roblox. Start with an HQ, mine ore and pump oil, build barracks, factories, airfields and docks, capture and grow cities, and research a tech tree across four eras.

Play a skirmish against up to five AIs with four personalities, or play online with friends: the host's browser runs the game and friends join with a room code, peer to peer, with no game server. Land, air and sea units, with a destroyer, battleship and submarine triangle at sea. On Pangaea and Lakes maps, a river splits the players into two sides, crossed by two stone bridges.

It has twists of its own: a government in exile, a last stand at the HQ, insurgency for knocked-out players, city contract auctions and bounties, coalitions and wanted aces. New players get First Orders, a guide that points at the very next click for the first six steps of any match, or can start with Boot Camp.
madeWith: TypeScript and Canvas 2D, no engine; online play is peer to peer over WebRTC. Code written with Claude Opus from my design docs; pixel art from PixelLab.

title: Verdant Relay
pitch: Scavenge by day. Hold the line by night. Loot an overgrown city, then defend the Relay with what you brought home.
number: 6 nights · loot only counts if you extract
about: You are a scavenger supplying Verdant Relay, a power-and-comms hub built into an overgrown transit station. By day you head out into a district: finish its objective, grab loot, then hold E in the extraction zone. Loot only counts if you get out.

By night you defend the Relay. Build towers on glowing pads, read the wave preview, and spend Intel to decrypt or sabotage what's coming. Survive six nights; the Canopy Colossus attacks on the last one. Research Data from every run buys permanent unlocks.
Stage 9 added real quests with a tracker and an arrow, skillful day combat (roll, deflect, punish openings), wooden bridges across the rivers, and towers you can build on any free tile at night.
madeWith: JavaScript and Three.js, rendered as pixel art. Code written with Claude Opus from my design docs; every sprite drawn pixel by pixel by Claude in build scripts.

title: Slipstream Salvager
pitch: A small, fast scrap robot rips parts off enemies at full speed and bolts them onto itself. Your movement is your weapon.
about: Six yards, about fifteen minutes, ending in a boss, The Compactor, that you take apart one move at a time. Only a hit at full speed does damage, and every part you tear off and bolt on changes how you move and attack: a Booster's Burn, Grip Treads that power-slide, Jump Jets, Springs, a Plow, Jaws.

You pick your route by driving out through exit gates whose signs show what you can salvage there. Three chassis to unlock by playing, two run modifiers, and a daily run with one seed a day that is the same for everyone.
madeWith: TypeScript and one HTML canvas, no engine. Code written with Claude Opus from my design docs; pixel art from PixelLab plus sprites Claude draws pixel by pixel in code.

title: Last Watt
pitch: A tower defense where energy is a live flow. Your towers are lights, and they fire on watts, not ammo.
number: 12 kW Lamp → 6 kJ/s, if the grid can feed it
about: An enemy's health is in kJ, and a Lamp drawing 12 kW does 6 kJ/s only if the grid can feed it. Build more towers than your Burners can run and the whole wall slows down together. Keep the Hearth lit for 12 waves, then see how long it lasts in endless.

Four maps, six towers with branching upgrades, and seven enemies that each hit the grid a different way: Shades cut Nodes, Snuffers put out Burners, Siphons drink from your lines. Each Node carries at most 60 kW, so where the power goes is a decision.
This one is a work in progress, built to find out whether the idea is fun. What you felt matters more than bugs.
madeWith: TypeScript and Canvas, no engine. Code written with Claude Opus from my design docs; pixel art from PixelLab plus sprites Claude draws pixel by pixel in code.

title: Trotline
pitch: You don't buy towers here. You catch them. Fish from the dock, then sell each catch or put it in the water to guard the smokehouse.
number: catch rate = zone × habitat × bait × reel
about: Thieves walk the road toward your smokehouse. Your defenders are what you pull out of the water: fish from the dock, then sell each catch or deploy it to guard the shore. Bait lures pull fish in, chum draws gulls and bears out where your rays can reach them.

A season is 12 waves. Send boats (a rowboat, a skiff and a trawler) to fish where you point them and bring the catch back to the live well. Every catch rate comes from one formula you can read: the zone, where the line sits, the bait, and the reel.
madeWith: TypeScript and Canvas, no engine. Code written with Claude Opus from my design docs; pixel art from PixelLab plus sprites Claude draws pixel by pixel in code.

title: Slipstream Salvager 3D
pitch: The same rules as Slipstream Salvager, seen from inside the little scrap robot. Speed is the weapon, and here you feel it.
about: The first-person version of Slipstream Salvager. Same rules, same scrapyards, same Rammers and Snappers. Only a hit at full speed (the claw glows teal) does damage. Hit an enemy where its part sits to tear it off, tow it behind you, bolt it on, and you move the way it did.

A Rammer's Booster turns your attack into its charge, a Snapper's Grip Treads let you power-slide round, a Plow makes your front a ram, Jaws bite on and sling you back out. Clear a yard, then drive out through the exit whose sign shows the part you want.
controls: Mouse or A/D (click the view first)
madeWith: TypeScript and Three.js. Code and low-poly models built with Claude Opus from my design docs.

title: Carpet Joint
pitch: Run the house on a neon 1970s strip. Write your own games' odds, work the floor live, and survive the swings, because the house doesn't always win.
about: You run the house. Click a table to see its paytable with every bet's exact house edge and hit rate, and change what a bet pays. The cage panel shows the Sweat: the chance the cage runs dry before 6am, from replaying the rest of tonight 500 times with the real paytables.
Right now this is the debug floor: a sawdust joint with two tables and a night's crowd walking in. Send in a whale and watch the Sweat move.
No real money, ever.
madeWith: TypeScript and one 640×360 canvas, deterministic 60 Hz sim. Code written with Claude Opus from my design docs; pixel art from PixelLab plus sprites Claude draws pixel by pixel in code.
